claims.claim: Le Guin says a novel gains its power less from the sound of any single sentence than from the pacing and rhythm of paragraphs and chapters.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "Reciprocity of Prose and Poetry" (1983), in Dancing at the Edge of the World (1989)
claims.quote: the pacing and rhythm of paragraphs and chapters

claims.claim: Le Guin praises a book she admires by calling its prose of unobtrusive excellence.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, blog 51, "The Narrative Gift as a Moral Conundrum", 2011
claims.quote: The prose is of unobtrusive excellence.

claims.claim: Le Guin says the sound and rhythm of prose is so different from poetry, being in a way much coarser.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin in conversation with David Naimon, excerpted from Ursula K. Le Guin: Conversations on Writing (Tin House, 2018), published at Literary Hub
claims.quote: the sound in the rhythm of prose, it is so different from poetry
claims.page: the poetry conversation, answer on Woolf and sound

claims.claim: Le Guin says the rhythms of a prose work are a very long beat.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin in conversation with David Naimon, Conversations on Writing (Tin House, 2018), excerpt at Literary Hub
claims.quote: long beat, the rhythms of a prose work
claims.page: the poetry conversation, answer on Woolf and sound

claims.claim: Le Guin says that, besides the long beat of the whole work, the sentence has its rhythms too.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin in conversation with David Naimon, Conversations on Writing (Tin House, 2018), excerpt at Literary Hub
claims.quote: Of course, the sentence has its rhythms too.
claims.page: the poetry conversation, answer on Woolf and sound

claims.claim: Le Guin says the deeper meaning that poetry shares with music is carried by the rhythm and the beat, the music of the sound.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin in conversation with David Naimon, Conversations on Writing (Tin House, 2018), excerpt at Literary Hub
claims.quote: it is the rhythm and the beat, the music of the sound that carries it
claims.page: the poetry conversation, answer on Macaulay and Swinburne

claims.claim: Le Guin says she does not think syllabically but rhythmically.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin in conversation with David Naimon, Conversations on Writing (Tin House, 2018), excerpt at Literary Hub
claims.quote: I don’t think syllabically, I think rhythmically.
claims.page: the poetry conversation, answer on haiku

claims.claim: Le Guin describes Annals of the Parish as the annual records of a parish minister, kept and dated year by year for 50 years, from 1760 to 1810.

claims.quote: kept and dated year by year for 50 years
claims.page: essay body, paragraph on the book's form

claims.claim: Le Guin calls the annalist narrator of that book a very old-fashioned narrator, and therefore reliable.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, "B-Sides: John Galt's Annals of the Parish", Public Books, 23 January 2017
claims.quote: a very old-fashioned narrator, and therefore reliable

claims.claim: Le Guin says the annalist leaves it up to the reader to hear what is being told, to imagine it and to feel it.

verdicts.trueWording: less from the sense and sound of any sentence or paragraph
verdicts.note: Raw full text of the book scan at ebin.pub; quote 'the pacing and rhythm of paragraphs and chapters' appears verbatim in 'Reciprocity of Prose and Poetry', on the page carrying the running head RECIPROCITY OF PROSE AND POETRY 109 (OCR 'log'), confirming p.109. The subject is the large-scale work the Silas Marner passage came from. Nuance recorded, not a defect: the page's small-unit side is 'any sentence or paragraph' (and includes 'sense' as well as sound), and the large-unit side also names the shape and pace of the actions described; the claim's narrower 'any single sentence' is contained within it.

verdicts.trueWording: The prose is of unobtrusive excellence.
verdicts.note: ursulakleguin.com blog 51 fetched live; sentence appears verbatim in the paragraph praising a book that 'brilliantly demonstrates a narrative gift in the service of clear thought, honest feeling, and passionate integrity' (unnamed in that paragraph; contrasted with Kathryn Stockett's The Help). Admiration limb is explicit. CITATION CORRECTION: the page dates the post May 2012 (Reading, Seeing ii), not 2011.

verdicts.trueWording: so different from poetry, because it's in a way much coarser
verdicts.note: lithub.com fetched live; quote appears verbatim in Le Guin's answer to the Woolf-and-sound question. The 'much coarser' limb is on the page but split across markup spans ('coarse'+'r'), so it renders correctly in a browser and is only invisible to a naive substring grep; verified in the raw HTML. Page's wording is 'the sound in the rhythm of prose', not 'sound and rhythm'.

verdicts.trueWording: It's a very long beat, the rhythms of a prose work
verdicts.note: lithub.com, same answer on Woolf and sound; quote 'long beat, the rhythms of a prose work' verbatim. Page order is inverted from the claim (predicate first) but both limbs hold.

verdicts.trueWording: Of course, the sentence has its rhythms too.
verdicts.note: lithub.com, same answer; sentence verbatim and immediately follows the long-beat sentence, so the claim's 'besides the long beat of the whole work' framing is supported by adjacency.

verdicts.trueWording: the rhythm and the beat, the music of the sound
verdicts.note: lithub.com; quote verbatim in the answer to the Macaulay/Swinburne question, locator correct. Page says the deeper meaning 'is where poetry approaches music' where the claim says 'shares with music' - same substance.

verdicts.trueWording: I don't think syllabically, I think rhythmically.
verdicts.note: lithub.com; verbatim (curly apostrophe on the page) in the answer about haiku and why the syllable count gives her no form. Locator correct.

verdicts.trueWording: is the principal problem that confronts a writer
verdicts.note: theanarchistlibrary.org fetched live; page header confirms Rob Maslen, Foundation: The Review of Science Fiction No. 67, Summer 1996. Quote 'recording a diversity of different understandings and ways of speaking' verbatim, in the Semley's-necklace section, within the clause 'for her, as for her mother Theodora Kroeber ... is the principal problem that confronts a writer, whether she is an archaeologist or a novelist'. Le Guin limb supported by the antecedent 'for her'; the page frames it as a writer's problem generally, and the claim's omitted tail is 'rooted in a particular time and place'.

verdicts.trueWording: kept and dated year by year for 50 years
verdicts.note: publicbooks.org fetched live; the whole sentence names the annual records of Mr. Balwhidder, minister of the parish of Dalmailing in Ayrshire, and the 1760-1810 span. Every limb verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: a very old-fashioned narrator, and therefore reliable
verdicts.note: publicbooks.org; sentence opens the Mr. Balwhidder paragraph verbatim, and the following sentences ('He will not, he cannot, mislead you') confirm the reliability limb.

publicbooks.org; verbatim, italicised in the paragraph beginning 'Whatever his annals tell of greed, cruelty, or hate', immediately preceding the account of the riot at the kirk (the claim's locator points one paragraph later than the sentence sits, which does not touch any limb).

verdicts.trueWording: It's left up to us to hear what's being told
verdicts.note: publicbooks.org; quote verbatim, continuing 'to imagine it, to feel it'. The page states it in the passive with no agent named; the agent named in the surrounding argument is Galt ('Galt tells without showing'), acting through his annalist narrator, whose own restraint ('All he says about it is...') is the mechanism - so the claim's 'the annalist leaves it up to the reader' is a supported gloss, not a page phrase.

verdicts.trueWording: in those few words, in their choice and in their cadence
verdicts.note: publicbooks.org; the page reads 'And all the material we need in order to hear, imagine, feel the scene is in those few words, in their choice and in their cadence.' Every limb verbatim; claim shifts 'we' to 'the reader'.

verdicts.trueWording: Galt's prose works like poetry: every word tells
verdicts.note: publicbooks.org; verbatim (italicised). The page joins the two limbs with a colon where the claim says 'because'; the colon carries the same causal force and the following quoted line illustrates it.

verdicts.trueWording: may yield psychological and anthropological insights of universal value
verdicts.note: publicbooks.org; the sentence 'Intimate knowledge of one small community may yield psychological and anthropological insights of universal value.' closes the small-town-novels paragraph (Cranford, Casterbridge, Lark Rise, Gopher Prairie, Holt). Locator correct, every limb verbatim.
